chapters.title: Chapter 3: American Options, Convergence, and Tree Limitations

lessons.title: Pricing American Options on a Tree: Backward Induction With Early Exercise

children.text: Chapter 1 made the case for why early exercise matters and walked through one small hand-built example. Chapter 2 built the complete, properly calibrated machinery, but only ever priced a European option with it. This lesson closes that gap with a single, precise change to the backward induction rule, the same change, in fact, that Chapter 1's Hind Metals example applied informally before the formal machinery existed to back it up.

Chapter 2's entire pipeline, calibrate u, d, and p, build the recombining lattice, discount backward, stays completely intact. Exactly one line changes, and it changes at every single non-terminal node.

body.caption: Chapter 2's one-step formula becomes the 'hold' side of a comparison. Intrinsic value is the same payoff function used at expiry, applied to this node's stock price instead.

children.text: Terminal nodes need no change at all, there is no 'hold' option once expiry has arrived, so the terminal value is just the payoff, identical for American and European trees. Every node before that, all the way back to today, gets this one extra comparison. Nothing about calibration, discounting, or the lattice's shape is touched.
Calls vs Puts: Where This Actually Bites

body.caption: Does early exercise ever change the price?

cells: Never optimal. American call price equals the European call price exactly
Can be optimal just before a dividend, forfeiting the dividend is the cost of continuing to hold
Can be optimal, this chapter's running example
Can be optimal, and typically more so than the no-dividend case

body.text: This chapter's Nifty tree, like Chapter 2's, does not model an explicit dividend yield on the index. Real Nifty options are affected by the dividends paid by the fifty companies underneath the index, handled in practice by subtracting a continuous dividend yield from the drift used to build u, d, and p. That refinement sits outside this course's scope, worth knowing exists before assuming a real index option behaves exactly like the dividend-free examples built here.

children.text: Applying It to Chapter 2's Nifty Tree

Reuse Chapter 2, Lesson 5's exact calibrated lattice, same S0 = 24,000, u = 1.02899, d = 0.97183, p = 0.5403, r = 6.5%, six steps, so every stock price at every node is already known. Only the payoff changes, from a 24,000-strike call to a 24,000-strike put, and the exercise check from Chapter 2's formula gets switched on.

body.caption: Terminal put payoffs, same lattice as Chapter 2, Lesson 5's call

children.text: One step back from these terminal payoffs, at the level with five steps remaining, the exercise check fires for the first time, and not at every in-the-money node either.

body.caption: Five steps remaining: hold value vs intrinsic value at every node

body.text: Deeper into this chapter's tree, at S = 23,323.85 with only one step remaining rather than five, the same in-the-money level no longer triggers exercise, hold there works out to 844.76 against an intrinsic value of only 676.15. More time remaining generally means more value in waiting, which is exactly why the exercise decision has to be checked fresh at every single node, not assumed from depth-in-the-money alone.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: In the five-steps-remaining table above, the node at 23,323.85 shows hold = 611.24 and intrinsic = 676.15. What determines the American value at this node?
options: Always the hold value, since American options prefer to wait
Always the intrinsic value, since the put is in the money
Whichever of the two is larger, here the intrinsic value of 676.15
The average of the hold and intrinsic values
body.explanation: The American backward induction rule takes the maximum of hold value and intrinsic value at every node. Here intrinsic (676.15) exceeds hold (611.24), so the American value is 676.15 and early exercise is optimal at this specific node. A node one step closer to today with the identical stock price would not necessarily make the same call, exactly what the callout above shows happening at 23,323.85 with only one step left.

body.title: The Call Side of the Same Tree
body.scenario: Suppose, instead of the Nifty put above, the same six-step lattice was used to price an American call struck at the same at-the-money level, on a single stock, not an index, that is confirmed to pay no dividends over the option's 3-month life.
body.prompt: Would you expect the exercise check to fire at any node in this tree? What price would you expect the American call to come out to?
body.modelAnswer: No, the exercise check should never fire. For a non-dividend-paying underlying, an American call is never optimally exercised early, exercising throws away both the option's remaining time value and the interest that could otherwise be earned by delaying payment of the strike. Since early exercise never happens, every node's American value equals its hold value, which means the American call price on this lattice would come out identical to Chapter 2, Lesson 5's already-computed European call price of ₹848.23, with no new computation actually required.

body.text: Pricing an American option on a tree is not a different algorithm from pricing a European one. It is the exact same backward induction, with one comparison, hold value against intrinsic value, inserted at every node. Whether that comparison ever actually changes the answer depends entirely on the option and the underlying, never on the tree-building machinery itself.

points: American pricing on a tree changes exactly one thing versus Chapter 2's European pipeline: every non-terminal node takes the maximum of its hold value and its intrinsic value.
Terminal nodes are unaffected, there is no hold option at expiry, so American and European trees always agree on the terminal payoffs.
An American call on a non-dividend-paying underlying is never optimally exercised early, so its price equals the European call price exactly, no early-exercise premium exists at all.
On the reused Nifty lattice, the American put priced at ₹513.26 against a European put's ₹461.38 on the identical lattice, an ₹51.88, roughly 11.2%, early-exercise premium.

Whether a specific node triggers early exercise depends on both how deep in the money it is and how much time remains, the same in-the-money stock level can trigger exercise with five steps left and not trigger it with only one step left.
